steps.observation: Work on this for 60 seconds; do not stop early. How does a transformer neural network work, conceptually?

steps.action:
Conceptual overview of a Transformer

1. What problem is it trying to solve?  
   Classical sequence models (RNNs, LSTMs) process tokens one-by-one in order. That makes it hard to (a) capture very long-range dependencies and (b) exploit modern parallel hardware. The Transformer replaces recurrent processing with a mechanism—self-attention—that lets every token look at every other token in the sequence in a single, highly parallelizable step.

2. How does a token “look” at the rest of the sequence?  
   Each token is first mapped to a vector, called an embedding. Three learned linear projections of that embedding are produced:  
   • Query vector q  
   • Key vector k  
   • Value vector v  
   To decide how much attention token i should pay to token j, take the dot product qi · kj, scale it, pass it through a softmax over all j. The resulting weights tell us how to form a weighted average of the value vectors. Mathematically, that’s Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QKᵀ/√d) V.

3. Multi-head attention: multiple sets of (Q,K,V) projections run in parallel (the “heads”). Each head can specialize in a different linguistic pattern (e.g., subject-verb agreement, coreference). The heads’ outputs are concatenated and linearly mixed.

4. Positional information: Since attention is permutation-invariant (tokens don’t come with an inherent order), we add positional encodings to the embeddings. These can be fixed sinusoids or learned vectors, allowing the model to know that “cat” came before “sat.”

5. Layer structure (encoder block)  
   a. Multi-head self-attention (all tokens attend to all tokens).  
   b. Add & Norm: a residual connection plus layer normalization.  
   c. Position-wise feed-forward network: two linear layers with a non-linearity (e.g., ReLU or GELU).  
   d. Another Add & Norm.  
   Stacking N of these blocks builds the encoder; stacking N more with slight tweaks (masked attention, cross-attention) builds the decoder for tasks like translation.

6. Encoder–decoder interaction (for seq-to-seq tasks)  
   • Encoder produces contextualized vectors for every source token.  
   • Decoder attends to its own past outputs (masked self-attention so it can’t peek at the future) and to the encoder’s outputs (cross-attention) to generate one target token at a time.

7. Why does it work well?  
   • Global receptive field at every layer: any token can relate to any other in one hop.  
   • Parallelism: all tokens processed simultaneously ⇒ faster training.  
   • Interpretability: attention weights reveal which parts of the input influenced a decision.  
   • Scalability: stacking more layers, heads, width, and data keeps improving performance (“scaling laws”).

8. Training vs. inference  
   During training, teacher forcing provides the ground-truth previous tokens; the model is optimized via back-prop on a cross-entropy loss. At inference, the decoder autoregressively samples or searches (beam, greedy) for the next token until a stop condition.

9. Variants and extensions  
   • BERT: encoder-only, trained with masked-language modeling.  
   • GPT: decoder-only, trained autoregressively.  
   • Vision Transformers: same idea applied to image patches.  
   • Long-sequence tricks: sparse attention, linearized attention, etc.

In short, a Transformer converts sequences into rich, context-aware vector representations by letting every element attend to every other element through scaled, multi-head self-attention, all while maintaining computational efficiency via massive parallelism.
